subject: Post-call: Codelane pilot economics & throttling levers — recap and next steps
messages:
From: Grace Oconnor <grace@redwood.com>
To: Amit Reddy <amit@codelane.com>, Elliot Jensen <elliot.j@codelane.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>, Diego Fernandez <diego@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 07 Jun 2026 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: Post-call recap: Codelane pilot economics & next steps

Hi Amit / Elliot — thanks for the time today. Quick recap from our call and proposed next steps so everyone is aligned.

Key pain points you shared
- Token spend volatility: peak inference spend during heavy validation runs causes surprise overages.
- Tight budget for Q3: you called out ~USD 60k ceiling for pilot windows that include peak tooling.
- Latency sensitivity on live verification flows: target ~150ms p95 for single-turn generation on a 512-token average.
- Session reuse patterns: many short-lived sessions but a handful of long-running validation jobs where caching could help.

Goals for a focused pilot
1) Demonstrate net token spend reduction of 30–45% via batching + prefix/KV caching in realistic workloads.
2) Meet or approach 150ms p95 latency for the primary verification route under expected concurrency.
3) Produce a simple TCO that shows unit economics (per-invocation) and projected QPS spend for a 90-day pilot.

Redwood action items (what we agreed to)
- Deliver initial TCO model and three scenario decks (conservative / expected / aggressive) — attachment: tco_model_codelane.xlsx
- Share a draft pilot SOW with deliverables, timeline, and success metrics — attachment: pilot_statement_of_work_v1.pdf
- Schedule a short technical demo of batching & prefix caching (showing expected token-savings on your trace) — propose Thu Jun 11, 10:00am PT
- Provide answers to the security/compliance checklist you flagged — attachment: codelane_security_q_and_a.pdf

Open questions for you
- Is the USD 60k budget per quarter or a hard cap for the whole pilot period?
- Can you share a sample request trace (anonymized) for the verification route so we can sanity-check cache hit assumptions?

Next steps
- I will circulate the TCO workbook and SOW by EOD Tue.
- Ben will prepare a short technical note on expected caching/batching levers and where we expect most wins.
- If Thu Jun 11 works, I’ll send a calendar invite and Ben will demo.

Thanks again — looking forward to moving this to an ops-ready pilot.

—
Grace Oconnor
Enterprise Account Executive, Redwood Inference
grace@redwood.com | +1 415-555-0132

Thanks Grace — solid summary. A couple quick clarifications from our side: 
- The USD 60k number is a hard cap for Q3 budget allocations; if the pilot is longer we can discuss reauthorization but treat it as the working constraint.
- I will pull together an anonymized request trace for the verification route and share early Tue.

Appreciate the attachments — looking forward to the SOW + demo.

Best,

Thanks — adding a few technical notes that will feed the TCO scenarios. Attaching a short demo notes file: batching-demo-notes.md.

Notes / assumptions
- Avg sequence length for verification: ~450 tokens (you confirmed ~300–600 depending on success/failure).
- Live verification is latency-sensitive; batching window should be conservative (target 8–12) to avoid p95 inflation for single-turn flows.
- For long-running validation jobs we expect sticky session patterns where prefix/KV cache hits could hit 50–70% on repeated prompts; for short sessions caching is lower.
- Suggested starting runtime config for pilot: dynamic batching target 10, max latency budget 200ms, prefix cache TTL 45s for verification route.
- Expected token reduction: 20–30% from batching alone in the conservative case; with prefix cache applied to validation jobs total reduction could reach 35–45% depending on session reuse.

Risks / tradeoffs
- If your live flows have significant per-request variability (very long tails) batching may add jitter; we can instrument and fall back to single-request paths for the highest-SLA routes.
- Quantization can reduce GPU cost but may require a short model-compatibility pass (we can include this in an ops appendix).

Action for us: I’ll seed the TCO with two operational scenarios (usage-first vs reserved capacity) and tag the variables where caching assumptions materially change the cost curve.

—
Ben Carter
